newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Latam oil demand growth offers retailing opps.
newsitem.headline: Latam oil demand growth offers retailing opps.

text.p: Multinational oil companies, suffering from poor downstream margins and meagre growth in their core markets, are watching Latin America's steep demand forecasts and liberalising markets with interest.
Strangely, analysts say the region will not need any more refineries to meet this demand, because there is enough spare capacity and potential to expand existing plants already.
But having perfected the high-margin retail forecourt in Europe and the United States, oil companies are keen to bolster their marketing businesses with new assets in Latin America.
Sondra Scott, oil analyst for Cambridge Energy Research in Mexico, expects Latin America to account for 18 percent of global incremental oil demand growth between now and 2005.

But, she says, "Until 2005, there wont be a need for grass- roots refinery in Latin America, despite all the plans you currently see... From a market perspective there are a lot of other options for the demand growth in the region."

A recent survey by Paris-based Enerfinance and Washington- based Petroleum Finance Corp (PFC) said Latin America led the world in terms of return on downstream assets at 15-17 percent, compared to Europe at 0-4 percent and the USA at 3-6 percent.
The same survey forecasted regional oil products demand to rise by at least three percent per year until 2005, equivalent to a 1.7 million barrels per day (bpd) rise to six million bpd.
CERA's Scott sees Brazil topping the demand growth table, accounting for a full six percent of world oil demand growth until 2005.

"Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru are engaged in a "taking- off" phase, where demand is mostly driven by road transportation, thus stimulating diesel demand. Brazil, however, is a particular case, given the fact that the decrease in alcohol production will be covered by gasoline demand," the Enerfinance/PFC survey said.
Brazil also has one of the more open markets in the region, the survey found, as price controls were lifted recently.
The survey identified Argentina and Chile as the most open oil industries in the region. "However," the report added, "the Chilean market has kept its oligopolistic structure."
Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Trinidad and Tobago all liberalised their distribution and marketing sectors, although price or marketing margin controls persist, the survey said.
Venezuela retained price controls and state monopoly over distribution, but state-owned Petroleos de Venezuela plans to introduce competition in the retail market soon.

The Mexican market, if it were opened to competition, presented the most room for growth in outlets, although Venezuela was close behind. "The number of stations in Mexico could well be multiplied by three if the market was opened to competition. The same remark applies to Venezuela, although to a lesser degree," the survey said.
Nine companies control 75 percent of the total number of service stations and 82 percent of total product sales. Other than the big state oil companies, Shell, Exxon and Texaco numbered among these.
The survey found the biggest retail margins in Brazil and Argentina, but high throughput levels and market concentration helped to lift profitability in lower-margin countries, it added.
